subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the scene scale and composition, placing the baby dragon sitting upright facing forward with a cat nearby and a broken egg shell to the side, then sketching out the skeleton hierarchy starting from hips through chest, neck, and head joints.

Now I'm working through the body geometry and coloring, defining a spine chain of 3D points along the back and a teal-to-butter countershaded scale pattern for the torso, building it as an ellipsoid shape with layered paint for the back and belly.

Naming the neck chain with tip "head", parented to the "chest" joint from the spine chain. Then I'm adding a jaw joint parented to head, plus skull, snout, and lower jaw geometry attached to the head and jaw joints.

Now I'm placing teeth as small cones on the upper and lower jaw, amber eyes with dark pupils, back-swept horns, tiny nostril spheres, and a spiraling wisp of translucent gray smoke made from shrinking spheres curling from the left nostril.

Shaping the skull, snout, and jaw as boxes with precise positions and joint pivots, then building the torso as a smooth sweep along a spine chain with a chubby belly radius profile and shared matte coloring.

For the belly shading I'm working out a custom paint function that detects forward-facing, downward-angled normals to blend in a lighter "butter" tone, creating a soft countershaded belly patch using smoothstep thresholds on normal direction.

I'm adding subtle sine-based banding to the belly color for a plate-stripe effect, then applying the same paint scheme to the neck sweep and head spheres for consistency. I'm weighing the chart-packing cost of using low-segment spheres across many body parts to keep the texture sheet manageable.

Now I'm working out the sitting pose for the hind legs, placing hip, knee, ankle, and toe joints so the thighs come forward and feet rest flat on the floor.

Setting ankle and ball joint positions for the leg chain, then using a catmull path with sweep for smooth skinning, mirroring the leg for the right side by negating x. Now I'm planning the arm joints—shoulder, elbow, wrist positions—for a front-facing pose with hands resting near the belly.

For the wings, I'm positioning oversized, half-folded attachments at the back shoulders, with a chain running from shoulder to elbow to wrist to create the extended rest pose.

Checking joint budget across spine, limbs, wings and fingers to stay under the 160 limit, then planning wing membranes as surfaces stretched between adjacent finger chains sharing the wrist root.

Still planning membrane layout...

Defining wing arm sweeps with tapered radii and round caps, adding a small claw cone at the wrist, and setting up the finger chains as single-span polylines. Now I'm starting the tail chain from the hips backward.

Working out the tail curve points, giving it a chubby tapered radius along five joints, and planning a flat spade shape at the tip that sits in the XZ plane like it's resting on the ground.

Still defining the spade outline coordinates...

I'm adjusting the tail geometry on bone "tail5," giving it orange color and a slight bevel, then rethinking the belly-paint logic so tail and legs use the surface normal's y-component instead of z for countershading.

Now I'm setting up torso and limb paints by countershading between scale color and a buttery belly tone, then plotting positions for soft orange spine cones running along the back of the neck and torso.

Working out spine placement down the tail...

Now thinking about the egg: placing it beside the dragon at roughly x=-0.22, z=0.10, sized a bit bigger than a typical house cat scale so the baby fits inside, with a broken top showing jagged shell built from a lathe profile over an intact lower shell.

For the jagged rim, I'll scatter small flattened cone shards around the top edge, tilted and rotated to face tangentially so the shell edge reads as cracked rather than smooth.

Now I'm placing the egg itself on the ground near the broken shell, giving it a cream base color "#efe3c8" with speckle paint using brown and olive-teal spots for texture, and setting the lathe to a faceted 12-segment profile for a slightly low-poly look. I'm also scattering a few extra flat shard pieces lying nearby to suggest fallen fragments.

Since the egg and shards need a bone to attach to for the pose system, I'm creating a dedicated "eggRoot" joint parented to the hips at the egg's position, so all these prop parts can bind there instead of awkwardly attaching to a limb joint that would move them unnaturally.

Tuning the hip and tail chain parenting, then working out the butt and chest radius profile so the sitting body's bottom meets the ground smoothly.

Still mapping out the chain...

Still shaping facial geometry...

Adjusting the jaw gap slightly so a thin red line shows between the teeth for a subtle open grin. Now I'm positioning the eyes as big amber spheres with darker pupil ellipsoids placed slightly forward and scaled for shape.

Placing a tiny white highlight sphere on each eye for shine, then skipping brow details for simplicity. For the horns, I'm defining cream-colored cones tilted outward and upward from the head, sizing their base radius and length, and working out how to position each cone's center along its tilted axis.

Adding dark nostril spheres at the snout tip, then building a curling wisp of smoke rising from one nostril using a short sequence of growing spheres in light gray tones that fade lighter as they ascend.

I'm skipping extra details like brow spikes, stubby ears, and neck frills to keep the design clean, focusing instead on torso and belly paint plates. I'm estimating the total painted surface area across the torso, tail, limbs, head, and egg to settle on a texel density of roughly 1 for the scale pattern so it reads consistently at the chosen scale and edge size.

Adding feet, toes, and claw geometry...

For a sitting pose, the thigh goes forward, the shin sweeps back-down to the ankle, then the foot points forward again, with the ankle around (0.085,0.035,0) and ball at (0.085,0.02,0.05). I'm keying radii along the leg from thigh to foot roughly [0.05,0.04,0.025,0.02] and checking that the ground contact points sit at the lowest y values for stability.

Now I'm placing the arm chain—shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand—with the hand ending in a small sphere resting on the ground, then adding three tiny claw cones pointing forward-down from the hand for fingers.

Checking arm placement against torso width, the shoulder and elbow sit slightly outside the body's front edge, which looks fine. Then I'm positioning the wing attachment point behind the shoulder and sketching out a wing chain that stretches quite wide—around 0.35 span per side—so I'll need to scale that down to match body proportions.

I'm checking the wing height against the dragon's head size and confirming the proportions read as oversized wings, then mapping out the membrane panels between fingers f1-f2, f2-f3, and f3-to-body line. I'm noticing there's still an uncovered region below the arm up to the body line that needs its own membrane triangle to avoid a gap in the wing surface.

I'll pass point arrays directly for path inputs, and for the m4 triangle with no weight chain I'll bind it to a named joint instead, like "wingShoulderL" or "wingElbowL" for the wing rig.

For fingers I'll keep each as a single-span chain parented to "wingWristL" rather than adding extra joints for bending, keeping things simpler. For the membrane material, I'll use an amber tone with a paint function that varies shading along and across the surface to suggest veining.

Adding finger tip cones, deciding which extra details to skip like eyebrows and ear fins, and settling naming conventions for mirrored body parts before starting the actual build code with imports for the geometry helpers.

Now I'm writing the paint functions for the body, blending scale colors with a lighter belly tone based on surface position and normal direction.

Now I'm setting up the builder structure, starting with the root joint and hips, then defining the spine chain using a catmull curve through three control points to form the spine1, spine2, and chest joints.

Next I'm sweeping the spine with a tapering radius function that varies smoothly along the chain for a natural torso shape, then adding a neck chain from the chest to the head using a simple polyline path, preparing to sweep that too.

Now I'm placing the head joint, adding a jaw joint angled forward, and building a skull as a scaled sphere geometry positioned above the neck to give it a slightly elongated, asymmetric shape.

Still shaping facial features...

Now I'm setting up the tail chain off the hips with five catmull points tapering in sweep radius from 0.055 down to 0.018, colored with the limb paint, starting near the butt. Then I'm positioning a spade shape at the tail's end, extruding it along the tangent direction of the last tail segment.

Adjusting the spade's anchor point to sit at the tail tip, attaching it to the "tail5" bone, and giving it an orange color with slight bevel. Now I'm laying out the spine positions along the back and neck, placing them to avoid overlapping with the wing roots.

Continuing down the spine, I'm working out the remaining points along the back curve down through the hips and into the tail, estimating each y/z coordinate by combining the path center with the radius offset at that segment.

Now I'm setting up the feather cones: scaling a base cone geometry by a size factor, computing each feather's center position by offsetting from its base point along its direction vector, and coloring them orange. I'm also placing the egg root object and checking its position against where the wing extends so they don't overlap.

For the egg shell, I'm defining the lathe outline points that trace the outer and inner profile of the shape, making sure the curve rises smoothly to a sharp rim and comes back down without self-intersecting, keeping the outer radius wider than the inner one throughout.

For the shattered fragments at the rim, I'm placing seven thin jagged cones around a circle at mid-rim radius, each scaled flat and rotated so the flattened face points radially outward — working out how scale and rotation compose means the flat axis ends up aligned with the radial direction once I rotate around y by the fragment's angle.

Now I'm applying a speckled eggshell paint texture with tan, brown, and rust spots scattered over a cream base, used consistently on both the shell and interior surfaces. For the broken shards scattered on the ground, I'm adding a few thin rotated boxes with slightly randomized tilts, using the same eggshell paint, plus planning a larger curved fragment piece.

Positioning one larger shard leaning against the egg's side with specific rotation so it sits naturally, keeping it above ground level. I'm also attaching the egg lathe geometry to its own bone and figuring out how bone weighting applies when a position is given directly rather than tied to a joint.

Now I'm writing a reusable wing-building function that takes a side parameter (left/right) and mirrors coordinates accordingly, generating a chain of three joints—shoulder, elbow, wrist—following a curved path from the chest outward, with the wrist acting as the wingtip.

Adding finger chains...

Still writing membrane connections...

Double-sided normals should be fine since the prism is closed, and chains with degenerate polyline edges can fall back to area-weighted averaging. I'm sketching out the TypeScript typing for tuples and curve inputs, a claw helper for cones at the wrist, smoke spheres, and a short part-creation helper, then finalizing everything for export.

Eye pupil orientation looks fine, and I'll skip the small crest cones between the horns to keep things simpler. Time to write the final output.
